metadata.title: Claude, Writing Hookify Rules.
metadata.purpose: Take apart how Claude decides which skill to fire: explain the description-matching mechanism (the SKILL.md YAML description field as the fuse), name the design trade-off (a flexible, natural-language trigger surface at the cost of exact-name determinism), and evaluate what fails when a description is written carelessly. Lands the carry-out that a skill fires when the request wording matches the description paragraph — not when the skill is named — and that a poorly-written description quietly stays off, without the miss ever surfacing to the user.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the skill's real description phrases; a request that matches fires reliably every time, a request that doesn't simply leaves the skill off)

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. You don't switch on a Claude skill by naming it — the skill's author writes a plain-language description paragraph, and Claude matches your request against that paragraph. Naming the skill is optional; matching the description isn't. So: how do you describe the task well enough to fire the right skill?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('name' -> 'describe') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A Claude skill is a folder with one file, SKILL.md — and near the top, in the YAML frontmatter, sits a description field: a plain paragraph saying exactly when to use the skill. They optimized this for zero-friction invocation: nothing to import, no exact string to memorize, no menu of installed skills to browse through. Say 'help me write a rule for hookify,' never naming any skill, and it still fires — the description paragraph is doing the matching, not you.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder opening to one file card; a paragraph card growing beneath it; a NAME tag fading out; a request bubble arrowing into the paragraph, landing with a checkmark

production_viz.label: The paragraph is doing the matching
production_viz.mechanic: A folder card labelled 'writing-hookify-rules' opens to reveal one file card, 'SKILL.md'. A paragraph card grows beneath it (a few placeholder lines). A 'NAME' chip fades out (recolored, not struck) since naming isn't required. A speech-bubble request, 'help me write a rule for hookify,' arrows into the paragraph card; it lights terracotta and a checkmark appears, with the line 'the paragraph is doing the matching, not you.'

beats.narration_text: Here's the mechanism. Claude reads your request against that description, word for word — no menu, no button, no name required. The writing-hookify-rules paragraph lists four real trigger phrases: 'create a hookify rule,' 'write a hook rule,' 'configure hookify,' 'add a hookify rule.' Watch the anchor. Ask something that lands inside that wording, and the match fires the skill — Claude opens SKILL.md and follows exactly what it says, step by step. The design choice is unusual: the skill's author writes the trigger surface, not the platform.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — four phrase chips lighting in turn; a request arrowing in; one chip recoloring; MATCH -> SKILL FIRES; a short step list ticking down

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — four real phrases, one match
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four chips fade in one at a time in a 2x2 grid, each holding one of the skill's real trigger phrases: 'create a hookify rule' / 'write a hook rule' / 'configure hookify' / 'add a hookify rule'. A request bubble, 'add a rule to hookify that blocks rm -rf,' arrows into the grid; the closest-matching chip recolors terracotta, a checkmark appears, and a 'SKILL FIRES' chip lights beneath. A short three-line step list ('read SKILL.md' / 'execute steps' / 'return result') ticks down in sequence. THIS EXACT GRID RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Ask again to add a hookify rule blocking a dangerous command, and the same match fires every time — same phrasing in, same skill out. Ask something unrelated — 'explain YAML in general' — and none of the four phrases match. The skill stays off; Claude still answers, just without this file's playbook. This works if you value flexible, natural-language triggering; it fails quietly if you need a request to fire the exact skill you had in mind every time. A carelessly-written description will silently miss the requests it was meant to catch — and you won't see the miss, because Claude will still hand you an answer, just not the one running through this file.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same four chips firing three times in a row; then a different request arrowing in with no chip lighting, NO MATCH, SKILL STAYS OFF, a small Claude still answers note

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same match, or none at all
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 GRID RETURNS, identical, firing 'SKILL FIRES' three times in a row against the same request. Then it clears and a different request bubble, 'explain YAML in general,' arrows into the same four dimmed chips — none light. A 'NO MATCH' label appears, then 'SKILL STAYS OFF' beneath the grid, with a small note to the side: 'Claude still answers.'

beats.narration_text: A skill fires when your words match its description paragraph — not when you name it. From there, Claude opens the file and follows exactly what it says. The description is the fuse; write it carelessly, and the skill you built quietly stays off.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm writing my own Claude skill and I want it to fire reliably on the right requests without misfiring on unrelated ones. (1) Explain how Claude decides whether to invoke a skill — what it reads from the SKILL.md frontmatter, how it matches my request against the description field, and when it chooses to fire versus answer without the skill. (2) Given the description below, tell me which requests will fire the skill, which will silently miss it, and which will misfire onto adjacent skills. (3) Rewrite the description so its trigger surface catches the intended requests and keeps unrelated ones off. Description: 'Use when the user wants to write a Claude Code plugin hook or configure hookify.' Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when two of your skills have overlapping trigger phrases — which one fires, is that resolution behavior documented anywhere, and how should the two descriptions be designed so they split the request space between them cleanly instead of stepping on each other.
